title: Taoist Texts: Ethical, Political, and Speculative
dateDisplay: Texts of various dates, collected and translated in 1884
attributionNote: Balfour's volume gathers ten Chinese texts in translation. The Tao Te Ching, the Yin Fu Ching and the Kan Ying Pien are canonical or widely circulated; the T'ai Hsi, Hsin Yin, Ta T'ung, Ch'ih Wen T'ung and Su Shu are short scriptures and tracts of the Daoist canon, and the extract from the Hung Lieh Chuan is a Han-dynasty anecdote about Huai-nan Tsze. The individual texts are anonymous or traditionally attributed; the volume is Balfour's.
description: Frederic Henry Balfour's collection was the first English anthology to treat Daoist scripture as a literature rather than a curiosity. It opens with his own translation of the Tao Te Ching and then prints the short classics that the temples actually used: the Yin Fu Ching on the harmony of the seen and the unseen, the T'ai Hsi and Hsin Yin Ching on the nourishing of life and the seal of the heart, the Ta T'ung Ching on the great harmony, the Ch'ih Wen T'ung and the Ch'ing Ching Ching on purity and the settling of the mind, the Su Shu, or 'Book of Rewards', and the Kan Ying Pien on retribution. Together they show the devotional and moral side of Daoism that the philosophical classics do not.
historicalContext: Balfour edited the North-China Herald in Shanghai and wrote on Chinese religion and literature for English readers. Trübner published the volume in London and Kelly and Walsh in Shanghai in 1884, when the Daozang was still almost unknown in Europe and the morality books were being printed by the million for household use. His translations are plain and sometimes stiff, but they made a body of scripture available a generation before Legge's appendixes.
availabilityNote: Complete for this volume. All ten texts are streamed from the Internet Sacred Text Archive at read time, one text per chapter. Balfour's introduction and the notes he prints with each text stand with it, as in the printed volume; the volume's front matter is not part of the work.
